questions.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution mentions that There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 148**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 148** of the Indian Constitution mentions the establishment of the **Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) of India**.
 
• The CAG is responsible for auditing all receipts and expenditures of the Government of India and the state governments, including bodies and authorities substantially financed by the government.
 
• The CAG is considered the guardian of the public purse and ensures accountability and transparency in the financial administration of the country.
 
• The CAG is appointed by the **President of India** and holds office for a term of **6 years** or until attaining the age of **65 years**, whichever is earlier.
 
• Article 148 ensures the **independence of the CAG** by providing safeguards such as fixed tenure, removal procedure similar to that of a Supreme Court judge, and salary charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of the Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG):**

 
 
• The CAG audits and reports on the accounts of the Union and State governments to ensure they are in compliance with laws and regulations.
 
• It examines whether expenditures were made for the intended purposes and whether the government’s financial transactions were conducted efficiently.
 
• The reports of the CAG are submitted to the **President of India** or the Governor of a state, who then table them in the respective legislature.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**
 
 
• **Articles 149-151** of the Indian Constitution further elaborate on the duties, powers, and responsibilities of the CAG.
 
• **Article 149:** Specifies the duties and powers of the CAG.
 
• **Article 150:** Provides that the accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept in the format prescribed by the President on the advice of the CAG.
 
• **Article 151:** Stipulates that the reports of the CAG on the accounts of the Union and the States shall be laid before the Parliament or the State Legislature.
 
 
 
• **Independence of the CAG:**
 
 
• The CAG is independent of the executive, and its authority is protected under the Constitution.
 
• Its salary and other conditions of service cannot be varied to its disadvantage after appointment.
 
• The CAG is removed from office in the same manner as a judge of the Supreme Court, which ensures its independence.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Reports by CAG:**
 
 
• The CAG has been instrumental in uncovering several financial irregularities, such as the **2G spectrum case** and the **coal allocation scam**.
 
• Such reports lead to corrective measures and reforms in governance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Other Articles:**

 
 
• **Article 142:** Grants the Supreme Court the power to pass any decree or order necessary to ensure complete justice.
 
• **Article 144:** Mandates all authorities, civil and judicial, in India to act in aid of the Supreme Court.
 
• **Article 146:** Deals with the conditions of service of officers and employees of the Supreme Court.
 
• None of these articles pertain to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, which is specifically covered under **Article 148**.
 
 
 
• **International Counterparts:**
 
 
• Countries such as the United Kingdom have similar institutions like the **National Audit Office (NAO)**.
 
• The United States has the **Government Accountability Office (GAO)**, which performs similar auditing functions.

questions.question: Which section of the Indian constitution ensure social and economic reforms in a country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Directive Principles of State Policy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are outlined in **Part IV** of the **Indian Constitution**, spanning from **Articles 36 to 51**. These principles serve as guidelines for the state to ensure **socio-economic reforms** and to establish a just society.

• The DPSP aim to promote **economic equality**, reduce the disparity between the rich and the poor, and provide for the welfare of citizens by ensuring access to resources, healthcare, education, and employment.

• These principles are **non-justiciable**, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts. However, they act as a guiding framework for the government to formulate laws and policies.

• Key provisions under DPSP include ensuring adequate means of livelihood, equitable distribution of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protection of children and youth, free legal aid, and promotion of education and public health.

• Some examples of socio-economic reforms influenced by DPSP include the implementation of the **Right to Education Act** (2009) and the establishment of schemes like **MGNREGA** and **National Food Security Act**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Fundamental Rights**: 

• These are outlined in **Part III** of the Indian Constitution and guarantee civil liberties to individuals, such as the **right to equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation**.

• They are **justiciable** and can be enforced through courts.

• Examples include **Article 14 (Right to Equality)** and **Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty)**.

• **Fundamental Duties**: 

• Added by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, and listed under **Article 51A**, these duties are non-justiciable and act as moral obligations for citizens.

• Examples include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, and protecting the environment.

• **Separation of Powers**: 

• This principle ensures that the **legislative, executive, and judiciary** function independently to maintain a system of checks and balances.

• It is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but is derived from its provisions to prevent abuse of power.

• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**:

• They are inspired by the **Irish Constitution** and aim to establish **economic democracy**.

• Some specific articles include:

• **Article 39(b):** Distribution of material resources to subserve the common good.

• **Article 41:** Right to work, education, and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, or sickness.

• **Article 47:** Duty of the state to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Relationship Between DPSP and Fundamental Rights**:

• While **Fundamental Rights** ensure individual freedoms, the **Directive Principles** focus on the collective welfare of society.

• In cases of conflict, courts have attempted to harmonize both. For instance, the **Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)** established that DPSPs cannot override Fundamental Rights but play a crucial role in governance.

• **Implementation Challenges**:

• The non-justiciable nature of DPSP makes their enforcement dependent on the political will of the government.

• Resource constraints and regional disparities often hinder their effective implementation.

questions.question: In July 2025, the 17th BRICS Summit was held in which of the following country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Brazil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **17th BRICS Summit** was held in **July 2025** in **Brazil**. ***Hence, option 4 is correct.***
 
• **BRICS** is a grouping of major emerging economies consisting of:
 
 
• **Brazil**
 
• **Russia**
 
• **India**
 
• **China**
 
• **South Africa**
 
 
 
• The summit focused on issues related to:
 
 
• **Global economic cooperation**
 
• **Trade and investment**
 
• **Climate change**
 
• **Multilateral reforms**
 
• **Global South cooperation**
 
 
 
• Brazil hosted the summit as part of the rotational chairmanship system followed by BRICS nations.
 
• **Option-wise Analysis:**
 
 
• **South Africa** – Hosted the 15th BRICS Summit in 2023.
 
• **Russia** – Hosted the 16th BRICS Summit in 2024.
 
• **India** – Not the host of the 2025 summit.
 
• **Brazil** – Hosted the 17th BRICS Summit in 2025. **Correct**.
 
 
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Brazil.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **BRICS** was originally formed as **BRIC** in **2006**, and **South Africa** joined the group in **2010**.
 
• The term **“BRIC”** was coined by economist **Jim O’Neill** of Goldman Sachs in **2001**.
 
• **BRICS countries** together account for a significant share of the world’s:
 
 
• **Population**
 
• **GDP**
 
• **Natural resources**
 
 
 
• The **New Development Bank (NDB)**, established by BRICS in **2014**, is headquartered in **Shanghai, China**.
 
• BRICS aims to strengthen cooperation among emerging economies and promote a more balanced global order.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **BRICS Summits** are held annually under the rotating presidency of member nations.
 
• Questions related to **international organizations, global summits, multilateral groupings, and current affairs** are frequently asked in competitive examinations.

questions.question: The Asian Development Bank was founded in ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1966**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Asian Development Bank (ADB)** was established on **19 December 1966**, with the objective of fostering economic growth and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region. 
• The founding members of ADB include **31 countries**, with the headquarters located in **Mandaluyong, Philippines**. 
• ADB focuses on **poverty reduction, sustainable development, and regional integration** through financial support, technical assistance, and policy consultation. 
• Its initial capital was **USD 1 billion**, and it has since grown significantly, with **more than 68 members** as of now, including both regional and non-regional members. 
• Japan and the United States are the **largest contributors** to ADB’s resources and play a crucial role in its governance and operations. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Functions of ADB:** 
• ADB provides **loans, grants, and equity investments** to its member countries for development projects in sectors like **infrastructure, education, health, and agriculture**. 
• It also offers **technical assistance** to help member nations design, implement, and improve development projects. 
• ADB promotes **regional cooperation** by supporting cross-border projects and encouraging trade and investment partnerships among member nations. 
• **Key Milestones:** 
• ADB’s first President was **Takeo Fukuda** from Japan. 
• It initiated its first loan project in **1968**, providing funds for agriculture development in Thailand. 
• Over the years, ADB has evolved to address challenges such as **climate change, disaster management, and urbanization**. 
• **Membership Details:** 
• ADB currently has **68 members**, with **49 regional members** and **19 non-regional members**. 
• Prominent members include **India, China, Japan, Australia, and the United States**. 
• **Funding Mechanism:** 
• ADB raises funds through **capital contributions** from member countries and by issuing bonds in international financial markets. 
• It also mobilizes resources from other financial institutions for co-financing development projects. 
• **Important Reports:** 
• ADB publishes the **Asian Development Outlook**, an annual report analyzing economic trends and prospects for its member countries. 
• The **Key Indicators for Asia and the Pacific** report provides statistical data to support regional development efforts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Japan’s Role:** Japan has been a significant contributor to ADB, reflecting its commitment to regional development. It holds the largest share of ADB capital along with the United States. 
• **Focus on Sustainability:** ADB emphasizes sustainable development through environmental conservation, renewable energy projects, and climate resilience initiatives. 
• **Recent Initiatives:** ADB launched a **COVID-19 Active Response and Expenditure Support (CARES) Program** to help member countries combat the pandemic. 
• **Headquarters:** The decision to set up ADB’s headquarters in the Philippines was influenced by its central location in the Asia-Pacific region.

questions.question: In June 2025, who has been re-appointed as the new CBDT Chairman?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ravi Agarwal**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Ravi Agarwal** has been re-appointed as the **Chairman of the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) in June 2025**. The CBDT is the apex body of the Income Tax Department in India. 
• The **CBDT Chairman** plays a critical role in formulating policies, overseeing tax administration, and ensuring compliance with tax laws in India. 
• **Ravi Agarwal** has previously served in several senior roles within the Income Tax Department, showcasing his expertise in tax administration and policy implementation. 
• The appointment of the CBDT Chairman is typically carried out by the **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC)**, which is headed by the Prime Minister of India. 
• This re-appointment reflects the government's confidence in **Ravi Agarwal's leadership** and his ability to steer the Income Tax Department effectively. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT):** 
• The CBDT is a statutory authority functioning under the **Department of Revenue**, Ministry of Finance, Government of India. 
• It is responsible for administering direct tax laws, including the **Income Tax Act, 1961**, and the **Wealth Tax Act, 1957** (now abolished). 
• The CBDT consists of a Chairman and six members, each of whom handles specific functions such as legislation, investigation, and taxpayer services. 
• **Responsibilities of the CBDT Chairman:** 
• Overseeing the administration of direct tax laws and ensuring **compliance with tax regulations**. 
• Formulating policies to improve tax collection and reduce tax evasion. 
• Supervising the functioning of the Income Tax Department across India. 
• Providing inputs for the annual Union Budget, particularly in matters related to taxation policies. 
• **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC):** 
• The ACC is responsible for appointments to the top posts in the government, including secretaries, additional secretaries, and directors of various departments. 
• It is chaired by the **Prime Minister**, with the **Home Minister** as a member. 
• The ACC ensures that appointments are made based on merit, experience, and the requirements of the respective departments. 
• **Recent Initiatives by CBDT:** 
• Introduction of the **Faceless Assessment Scheme** to enhance transparency and efficiency in tax administration. 
• Implementation of the **Taxpayer Charter** to ensure accountability and safeguard taxpayer rights. 
• Promotion of e-filing and digital platforms to simplify tax compliance for individuals and businesses. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **CBDT's Role in Economic Policy:** 
• The CBDT plays a pivotal role in shaping India's **tax policies** and ensuring their alignment with the nation's economic goals. 
• It works closely with other government departments to facilitate **ease of doing business** and attract foreign investments. 
• **Notable Predecessors:** 
• Several former CBDT Chairpersons have contributed significantly to modernizing India's tax system, including the introduction of GST and digital tax platforms. </ul

questions.question: In July 2025, ___________ was arrested in connection with the Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank Limited (ANSCBL) Ioan irregularities case.

The correct answer is __**Kuldeep Sharma**__.

__

• **Kuldeep Sharma** was arrested in connection with the **Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank Limited (ANSCBL) loan irregularities case** in **July 2025**.

• The loan irregularities case involved alleged misuse of funds and fraudulent activities in the functioning of **ANSCBL**, a cooperative bank operating in the union territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

• Authorities conducted thorough investigations and found evidence linking **Kuldeep Sharma** to these irregularities, leading to his arrest.

• The case highlighted issues in the management and oversight of cooperative banks, emphasizing the need for stricter regulations and accountability mechanisms.

• This incident is part of a broader effort to address corruption and financial misconduct within cooperative banking institutions in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Andaman and Nicobar State Cooperative Bank Limited (ANSCBL):** 

• **ANSCBL** is a cooperative banking institution operating in the union territory of **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**.

• It provides financial services to local residents, including loans for agricultural and small-scale industrial activities.

• Cooperative banks like ANSCBL aim to promote local economic development by offering accessible financial solutions.

• **Loan Irregularities:** 

• Loan irregularities typically involve activities such as **fraudulent loan approvals**, misuse of funds, and failure to adhere to banking regulations.

• Such practices undermine the credibility of banking institutions and can lead to significant financial losses.

• **India’s Cooperative Banking Sector:** 

• Cooperative banks in India operate under dual regulation by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and respective state governments.

• They play a crucial role in providing financial services to rural and semi-urban areas.

• Challenges in this sector include **governance issues**, lack of transparency, and limited access to technology.

• **Regulatory Measures:** 

• To address financial misconduct, the **RBI** has implemented stricter guidelines for cooperative banks.

• Recent reforms aim to improve the **transparency**, efficiency, and accountability of these institutions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Cooperative Banks in India:** 

• They are established under the **Cooperative Societies Act** and primarily cater to rural and semi-urban areas.

• These banks provide loans for agricultural and small-scale industrial activities, promoting local economic growth.

• **Legal Framework:** 

• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** monitors cooperative banks to ensure compliance with banking regulations.

• Stringent measures are taken to address instances of financial misconduct and irregularities.

• **Recent Banking Reforms:** 

• Reforms focus on improving governance, introducing technology-driven solutions, and enhancing customer trust.

• Emphasis is placed on greater accountability and transparency in banking operations.

questions.question: In the Union Budget 2025-26, there has been a plan establish _________- Day Care Cancer Centres in 2025-26.

 __

• **Day Care Cancer Centres:** These centres aim to deliver accessible and affordable cancer treatment, particularly for patients requiring chemotherapy or other day procedures, reducing the burden on larger hospitals. 
• **Healthcare Accessibility:** The move focuses on decentralizing cancer treatment, ensuring that patients in remote and underserved areas can access essential healthcare services without traveling long distances. 
• **Collaborative Efforts:** The initiative is likely to involve collaboration between the government and private entities, ensuring high-quality services and efficient operations.

 __

• They help in reducing **hospital congestion** and improving patient convenience. 
• **Government Initiatives for Cancer Care:** 
• The Indian government has launched schemes like the **Ayushman Bharat**, which covers a range of treatments, including cancer care, for economically weaker sections. 
• It has also emphasized the need for early detection and preventive measures through public awareness campaigns. 
• **Challenges in Cancer Care:** 
• India faces challenges such as **limited infrastructure, shortage of oncologists**, and low awareness about early detection. 
• The establishment of Day Care Cancer Centres is a targeted approach to address some of these challenges, especially in semi-urban and rural areas. 
• **Examples of Similar Initiatives:** 
• Countries like **USA and UK** have successfully implemented Day Care Centres for cancer care, ensuring comprehensive treatment and patient comfort. 
• Such centres have proven to be cost-effective and efficient in delivering specialized healthcare services. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Focus on Non-Communicable Diseases:** Cancer and other non-communicable diseases have been a growing concern, prompting government initiatives to address them effectively. 
• **Potential Benefits:** With the establishment of Day Care Cancer Centres, patients can expect **reduced waiting times, better access to treatment**, and improved quality of care. </ul

questions.question: National Infrastructure Readiness Index (NIRI) was launched in _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mon Apr 01 2024 00:00:00 GMT+0530 (India Standard Time)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **National Infrastructure Readiness Index (NIRI)** was launched on **Mon Apr 01 2024**. This initiative is aimed at assessing the readiness of infrastructure across various sectors.

• The **NIRI** evaluates critical infrastructure such as transportation systems, energy grids, water supply systems, and urban planning frameworks.

• The index provides a comprehensive analysis of the **current state of infrastructure development** and highlights areas needing improvement for sustainable growth.

• The launch date aligns with the government's **strategic planning** for infrastructure development in the financial year 2024-2025.

• **NIRI** is a tool intended to guide policymakers, investors, and stakeholders in making informed decisions regarding infrastructure investment and development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Purpose of NIRI:** 

• **National Infrastructure Readiness Index** aims to assess the preparedness of infrastructure to support economic growth and social development.

• The index is designed to monitor progress in infrastructure development and identify gaps in planning, execution, and maintenance.

• **Key Features:** 

• The index focuses on **sustainability, efficiency, and resilience** of infrastructure systems.

• It includes metrics for evaluating urban infrastructure, rural connectivity, and environmental impact.

• The data collected is analyzed and shared in reports to assist in strategic planning and policymaking.

• **Applications of NIRI:** 

• **Policy Formation:** Provides insights for government bodies to formulate effective infrastructure policies.

• **Investment Guidance:** Helps investors identify viable projects and areas with high growth potential.

• **Performance Benchmarking:** Enables comparison of infrastructure readiness across regions and sectors.

• **Global Relevance:** 

• India’s focus on infrastructure readiness aligns with global efforts such as the **United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).**

• The index supports India's commitment to **economic progress**, improving quality of life, and addressing climate change challenges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Launch Date:** **April 1, 2024**, marks the beginning of the financial year, making it an opportune time to introduce initiatives for economic planning.

• **Strategic Importance:** The index serves as a foundational step to evaluate and enhance India's infrastructure capabilities.

• **Sectoral Impact:** The infrastructure readiness index is expected to improve sectors like transportation, energy, water supply, and urban planning.

• **Government Focus:** The launch aligns with India’s increasing emphasis on infrastructure development, which is a critical driver for economic growth and job creation.

questions.question: Salkhan Fossil Park is in ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Salkhan Fossil Park** is located in the **Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh**, India.

• It is one of the most prominent fossil parks in the country, famous for its **marine fossils** that date back approximately **1.4 billion years**.

• The fossil park showcases specimens from the **Proterozoic Eon**, making it a significant site for studying early life on Earth.

• The fossils primarily include **stromatolites**, which are layered sedimentary formations created by the activity of ancient cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).

• Salkhan Fossil Park is a major site of interest for **geologists, paleontologists, and tourists** due to its unique and ancient fossilized formations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Proterozoic Eon:**

• The Proterozoic Eon spans from approximately **2.5 billion years ago to 541 million years ago**.

• It is characterized by the accumulation of oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere, known as the **Great Oxidation Event**.

• Stromatolites, found in Salkhan Fossil Park, are among the most significant fossils from this era, providing evidence of early microbial life.

• **Stromatolites:**

• Stromatolites are layered structures formed by the trapping, binding, and cementation of sedimentary grains by biofilms of microorganisms, primarily cyanobacteria.

• They are considered one of the earliest records of life on Earth, dating back over **3.5 billion years**.

• These formations are crucial for understanding the evolution of life and the Earth’s biosphere.

• **Sonbhadra District:**

• Sonbhadra is located in the southeastern part of Uttar Pradesh and is known as the **“Energy Capital of India”** due to its abundance of coal and thermal power plants.

• The district is rich in natural resources and has significant geological and archaeological importance.

• **Importance of Fossil Parks:**

• Fossil parks like Salkhan play a vital role in **educating the public** about Earth’s history and the evolution of life.

• They are also important for **scientific research**, helping to uncover details about ancient ecosystems and climatic conditions.

• Fossil parks contribute to **geotourism**, attracting tourists and boosting the local economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Geotourism:**

• Geotourism is a form of tourism that focuses on a destination’s geology and landscape as the primary attractions.

• It promotes conservation and awareness of geological heritage while supporting sustainable economic development in local communities.

• **Other Fossil Parks in India:**

• **Ghughua Fossil Park** in Madhya Pradesh – Known for its plant fossils, including palm, neem, and date trees, dating back to the Eocene epoch.

• **Akal Wood Fossil Park** in Rajasthan – Contains fossilized tree trunks from approximately 180 million years ago.

• **Significance of Fossils:**

• Fossils provide crucial information about past life forms, environmental conditions, and evolutionary processes.

• They are used in **biostratigraphy** to date rock layers and understand the chronological sequence of Earth’s history.

questions.question: What important event is celebrated during the festival of 'Baisakhi' in Chandigarh?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Founding of Khalsa Panth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Baisakhi** is one of the most significant festivals celebrated in **Punjab** and particularly in Chandigarh, marking the formation of the **Khalsa Panth** by **Guru Gobind Singh Ji** on **April 13, 1699**.

• The **Khalsa Panth** was founded to instill unity and courage among the Sikh community and to uphold the principles of righteousness and justice.

• On this day, Guru Gobind Singh Ji initiated the **Panj Pyare** (The Five Beloved Ones), who symbolized the spirit of sacrifice and devotion to the Sikh faith.

• The festival also coincides with the traditional harvest festival in Punjab, marking the beginning of the **harvesting season** for crops like wheat.

• Sikhs visit **Gurdwaras**, participate in religious processions, and perform **Kirtans** and prayers, followed by community meals or **langars**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Significance of Khalsa Panth:**

• The **Khalsa** represents purity and dedication to the Sikh faith. Members of the Khalsa Panth are expected to follow the **Five Ks**: Kesh (uncut hair), Kara (iron bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarments), and Kirpan (ceremonial sword).

• The initiation into Khalsa Panth is marked by the **Amrit Sanchar ceremony**, where individuals commit to the principles of Sikhism.

• **Harvest Festival:**

• Baisakhi is celebrated as a **harvest festival** in Punjab, marking the end of the Rabi crop season and the start of the new agricultural year.

• Farmers express gratitude to God for a good harvest and pray for prosperity in the coming year.

• **Historical Context:**

• The founding of the Khalsa Panth was a response to the persecution faced by Sikhs and other communities under oppressive regimes, particularly during the Mughal era.

• Guru Gobind Singh Ji aimed to create a community of warriors and saints who would stand against injustice and protect the oppressed.

• **Other Celebrations:**

• Besides its religious significance, Baisakhi is celebrated with cultural activities like **Bhangra** and **Gidda** (traditional Punjabi dances).

• Fairs and processions are organized in various parts of Punjab and Chandigarh, attracting people from different communities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Guru Gobind Singh Ji:** The 10th Sikh Guru, who played a pivotal role in shaping Sikhism and introduced the Khalsa tradition.

• **Panj Pyare:** The first five members of the Khalsa, representing the collective strength, unity, and commitment of the Sikh community.

• **Harvest Connection:** The festival aligns with the agricultural calendar, highlighting its importance in the agrarian society of Punjab.

• **Global Observance:** While primarily celebrated in India, Baisakhi is also observed by the Sikh diaspora worldwide, emphasizing its universal appeal within the Sikh faith.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following was the aim of Liberalisation under New Economic Policy 1991 of India?

options.text: To put embargo on enemy countries trade.
To increase restrictions on economic activities.
To open various sector of the economy.
To increase non-tariff barrier on Imports.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To open various sectors of the economy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Liberalisation** under the **New Economic Policy (1991)** aimed to reduce government control over the economy and encourage private sector participation. The goal was to make the economy more globally competitive.
 
• The policy involved removing excessive **restrictions, licenses, and quotas**, enabling businesses to function more freely without extensive bureaucratic interference.
 
• The liberalisation measures focused on **opening various sectors** to foreign investment, encouraging private companies, and eliminating trade barriers such as excessive tariffs and import restrictions.
 
• The **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1991** reduced the number of industries requiring compulsory licensing and allowed private participation in sectors previously reserved for the public sector.
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** was encouraged by easing regulations, enabling foreign companies to invest in industries like telecom, IT, and manufacturing, contributing to rapid economic growth.
 
• Liberalisation helped integrate India’s economy with the **global economy**, allowing Indian industries to compete on an international scale and attract foreign businesses and technologies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **New Economic Policy of 1991:**

 
 
• The New Economic Policy was introduced by the **Government of India** under the leadership of **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• It marked a **paradigm shift** in India’s economic strategy, moving away from protectionism towards liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG).
 
 
 
• **Impact of Liberalisation:**
 
 
• Liberalisation fostered **economic growth** by increasing competition and efficiency in industries.
 
• Encouraged the entry of **multinational companies** and facilitated access to advanced technologies.
 
• Created opportunities for **employment**, particularly in sectors like IT, telecom, and services.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Trade Policy:**
 
 
• Liberalisation reduced **import tariffs** and allowed easier import/export of goods.
 
• Enabled businesses to access **global markets**, expanding their scope and reducing dependency on domestic demand.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Economic Policies:**
 
 
• **Privatisation**: Focused on transferring ownership from public to private entities to enhance efficiency and profitability.
 
• **Globalisation**: Aimed at integrating India’s economy with the world economy through trade, investment, and cultural exchange.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sectoral Changes:**

 
 
• **Telecom:** Liberalisation allowed private companies to enter the telecom sector, boosting connectivity and innovation.
 
• **IT Industry:** Liberalisation led to the rise of the IT sector, making India a global hub for software development and services.
 
• **Manufacturing:** Encouraged the entry of foreign companies, leading to better technologies and higher productivity.
 
 
 
• **Challenges:**
 
 
• Liberalisation led to increased competition, which posed challenges for smaller and domestic industries.
 
• Concerns over the **uneven distribution of benefits**, with urban areas benefiting more than rural areas.
 
• Economic reforms required balancing growth with social equity and environmental sustainability.

questions.question: Which of the following was the British East India Company's first major victory in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Battle of Plassey**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Battle of Plassey** took place on **23 June 1757** between the forces of the British East India Company led by **Robert Clive** and the Nawab of Bengal, **Siraj-ud-Daulah**. 
• The battle was fought near **Plassey**, located in present-day **West Bengal**, along the banks of the Bhagirathi River. 
• The British East India Company secured a decisive victory due to the betrayal by **Mir Jafar**, the commander of Siraj-ud-Daulah's army, who sided with the British. 
• This victory marked the beginning of **British political dominance** in India, as it paved the way for the establishment of British control over Bengal and later other parts of India. 
• The **Battle of Plassey** is widely regarded as the **first major victory** of the British East India Company in India, setting the foundation for their empire in the subcontinent. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Battle of Ambur:** 
• The **Battle of Ambur** was fought in **1749** between Anwaruddin Khan, the Nawab of Arcot, and the combined forces of Chanda Sahib and the French. 
• It marked the beginning of French involvement in Indian politics but was not a major victory for the British East India Company. 
• **Battle of Wandiwash:** 
• The **Battle of Wandiwash** took place in **1760** between the British and the French during the **Third Carnatic War**. 
• It was a significant victory for the British, leading to the end of French ambitions in India. However, this occurred after the Battle of Plassey. 
• **First Anglo-Maratha War:** 
• The **First Anglo-Maratha War** occurred between **1775 and 1782**. 
• The war ended with the Treaty of Salbai, and it was not a major victory for the British East India Company. 
• **Significance of the Battle of Plassey:** 
• The Battle of Plassey allowed the British East India Company to gain control of Bengal's immense **wealth** and resources, strengthening their position in India. 
• It led to the installation of **Mir Jafar** as the puppet Nawab of Bengal, ensuring British dominance in the region. 
• The revenue from Bengal helped the British finance their wars and expand their presence in other parts of India. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Robert Clive:** 
• Robert Clive, often called "Clive of India," was the British commander who led the forces during the Battle of Plassey. 
• He played a crucial role in establishing British supremacy in India. 
• **Mir Jafar:** 
• Mir Jafar's betrayal of Siraj-ud-Daulah was instrumental in the British victory at Plassey. 
• He was later installed as the Nawab of Bengal but remained under British influence. 
• **Economic Impact:** 
• The victory at Plassey provided the British East India Company access to Bengal's **resources**, including its lucrative **trade routes** and **wealth**. 
• The Company began collecting **taxes directly** from Bengal, significantly boosting its financial strength. 
• **Political Impact:** 
• The battle marked the beginning of **British colonial rule** in India. 
• The Company's influence expanded from Bengal to other parts of India, eventually leading to the establishment of the British Empire in India. </ul

questions.question: Which bill/act provided for the trial of British or European persons by Indians, and sought equality between British and Indian judges?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ilbert Bill of 1883**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Ilbert Bill** was introduced in **1883** by **Sir Courtenay Ilbert**, the Law Member of the Viceroy's Council during the tenure of **Lord Ripon**, the then Viceroy of India. 
• This bill proposed to allow **Indian judges** to preside over cases involving British and other European subjects in India, ensuring **judicial equality**. 
• The bill aimed to **abolish racial discrimination** in the Indian judicial system and was a major step toward **legal equality** between Indians and Europeans. 
• However, the bill faced **strong opposition** from the European community in India, who saw it as a threat to their privileged position. 
• Due to the backlash, the bill was **amended**, which led to a compromise. The amended version allowed European subjects to request a jury with at least half of its members being Europeans. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Background of the Ilbert Bill:** 
• Before the Ilbert Bill, the judicial system in India was **highly biased**, with British subjects being tried only by British judges. 
• The bill was part of Lord Ripon’s broader vision of **liberal reforms** and efforts to grant Indians more authority in governance. 
• **Impact of Opposition:** 
• The opposition to the Ilbert Bill highlighted the **deep-seated racial prejudices** among the European settlers in India. 
• The agitation against the bill reinforced the divide between Indians and Europeans, leading to a **greater nationalistic awakening** among Indians. 
• **Lord Ripon’s Legacy:** 
• Lord Ripon is remembered as the **“Father of Local Self-Government in India”** for his efforts to empower Indians in administrative roles. 
• Other notable reforms during his tenure include the **reduction of press restrictions** and the introduction of local self-governance. 
• **Significance of the Ilbert Bill:** 
• The Ilbert Bill controversy was a pivotal moment in Indian history, as it **exposed the discriminatory policies** of the British and inspired early nationalist movements. 
• It also encouraged Indians to **fight for equality and self-governance** through organized efforts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Regulating Act of 1773:** 
• This act established the **Supreme Court of Judicature** in Calcutta and marked the beginning of the British judiciary in India. 
• It did not address the issue of judicial equality between Indians and Europeans. 
• **Pitt’s India Act of 1784:** 
• This act primarily dealt with the **administrative control** of the East India Company and did not involve judicial reforms. 
• **Indian Councils Act of 1892:** 
• This act was aimed at expanding the **legislative councils** and increasing Indian participation in governance but had no relevance to judicial matters.

questions.question: In 1991, rupee was devalued in two stages and the cumulative devaluation was about ___________ percent in USD terms.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**18 percent**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• In **1991**, the Indian rupee was devalued in two stages to address the **severe balance of payments (BoP) crisis**.

• The cumulative devaluation of the rupee was approximately **18 percent in USD terms**. This was undertaken to stabilize the economy.

• The devaluation was implemented under the leadership of then **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**.

• The move was part of a broader economic reform package aimed at liberalizing the Indian economy and moving towards a **market-driven exchange rate system**.

• This decision was crucial in restoring investor confidence and attracting foreign capital, thereby averting a financial crisis.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Background of the 1991 Economic Crisis:**

• India faced a **severe BoP crisis** in 1991 due to dwindling foreign exchange reserves, rising imports, and falling exports.

• Foreign reserves were so low that they could barely cover **three weeks of imports**.

• The Gulf War of 1990–1991 aggravated the crisis by increasing **oil prices** and reducing remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf region.

• **Steps Taken During the Crisis:**

• India secured loans from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**, but these were conditional on implementing structural reforms.

• The government initiated the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** reforms to open up the economy.

• The devaluation of the rupee was a key measure to make Indian exports more competitive and reduce the trade deficit.

• **Impact of the Rupee Devaluation:**

• The devaluation boosted **exports** by making Indian goods cheaper in international markets.

• It helped in **stabilizing foreign reserves** and restoring macroeconomic stability.

• The move also paved the way for long-term economic reforms, transforming India into a **market-driven economy**.

• **Key Figures Behind the Reforms:**

• **P.V. Narasimha Rao:** As the Prime Minister, he spearheaded the economic reforms and provided political backing.

• **Dr. Manmohan Singh:** As the Finance Minister, he played a pivotal role in formulating and implementing the reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Devaluation Process:**

• The first stage of devaluation occurred on **July 1, 1991**, when the rupee was devalued by approximately **9 percent**.

• The second stage followed on **July 3, 1991**, with an additional devaluation of around **9 percent**.

• **Exchange Rate Changes:**

• Before devaluation, the exchange rate was approximately **17.90 INR/USD**.

• After the devaluation, it increased to around **23 INR/USD**, reflecting an 18 percent cumulative change.

• **IMF Loan Conditions:**

• The devaluation was a precondition for receiving financial assistance from the **IMF**.

• Other conditions included **fiscal discipline**, reduction in subsidies, and promotion of foreign investment.

questions.question: Which of the following Indian states does not have a Legislative Council?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajasthan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Legislative Council** is the upper house in states with a bicameral legislature, while the Legislative Assembly is the lower house.

• Currently, only **six Indian states** have a Legislative Council: **Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka.**

• **Rajasthan** does not have a Legislative Council and follows a unicameral legislative system, with only a Legislative Assembly.

• The Legislative Councils in states are established under **Article 169** of the Indian Constitution.

• Creating or abolishing a Legislative Council requires a resolution passed by the Legislative Assembly of the state, followed by a parliamentary approval.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Legislative Council in India:** 

• The Legislative Council is also known as the **Vidhan Parishad**, and its members are called MLCs (**Members of Legislative Council**).

• The members of the Council are elected, nominated, or appointed through various methods such as elections by Legislative Assembly members, graduates, teachers, and local authorities.

• It serves as a revising chamber for bills passed by the Legislative Assembly and also provides expertise on policy matters.

• **Unicameral and Bicameral Legislature:** 

• **Unicameral legislature** refers to states with only one legislative body, the Legislative Assembly.

• **Bicameral legislature** includes states with two houses: the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.

• Examples of bicameral states include **Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra**, while states like **Rajasthan** follow a unicameral structure.

• **Article 169 of the Indian Constitution:** 

• This article provides the procedure for creating or abolishing the Legislative Council in a state.

• A state assembly must pass a resolution by a **special majority** (two-thirds of members present and voting) to initiate this process.

• The Parliament then enacts a law for the creation or abolition of the Legislative Council.

• **Historical Context:** 

• Initially, several states like Rajasthan, Punjab, and West Bengal had Legislative Councils, but they were later abolished due to financial and administrative concerns.

• The abolition of Legislative Councils is often debated due to concerns over their **effectiveness and necessity.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Structure of State Legislature:** 

• The Constitution of India allows states to choose between a unicameral and bicameral legislative system.

• States with a unicameral system only have a Legislative Assembly, which handles law-making and governance.

• Bicameral states have an additional house, the Legislative Council, which functions similarly to the Rajya Sabha at the national level.

• **Advantages of Legislative Council:** 

• Provides a platform for experienced individuals to contribute to law-making without contesting elections.

• Serves as a check and balance mechanism for bills passed by the Legislative Assembly.

• Facilitates representation for specific groups such as teachers and graduates.

• **Disadvantages of Legislative Council:** 

• Often criticized for being redundant and delaying legislative processes.

• Involves additional financial burdens on the state government.

• Its necessity and functionality are debated, especially in states with limited financial resources.

questions.question:
Which of the following statement is correct regarding the article 253 of Indian Constitution?

I. It is found in Part XI of the Constitution.

II. It relates to the Legislation for giving effect to international agreements.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Article 253** of the **Indian Constitution** is located in **Part XI**, which deals with the **relations between the Union and the States**. *Hence, statement I is correct.* 
• It empowers **Parliament** to make laws for the entire country or any part of it to implement **international treaties, agreements, or conventions**. *Hence, statement II is correct.* 
• This article allows the Parliament to legislate even on subjects in the **State List**, if required to fulfill international obligations. 
• The legislative power under Article 253 is derived from the principle of **federal flexibility** in India’s Constitution. 
• Examples include laws made to fulfill obligations under **international agreements** like the **UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change)** or treaties related to human rights. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Part XI of the Indian Constitution:** 
• Part XI deals with the **distribution of legislative and administrative powers** between the Union and the States. 
• It includes Articles **245 to 263**, covering topics such as the extent of laws made by Parliament and state legislatures and coordination between the Union and States. 
• Article 253 is located within this part and highlights the flexibility of legislative powers for international obligations. 
• **International Treaties and Agreements:** 
• India, as a signatory to several **international conventions**, requires domestic laws to ensure compliance. 
• Examples include the **Environmental Protection Act** (1986) implemented to fulfill obligations under **international environmental agreements**. 
• Parliament can make laws on subjects in the **State List** to meet these obligations under Article 253. 
• **Federal Flexibility:** 
• The Indian Constitution is characterized by a strong center, allowing the Union Parliament to legislate on subjects normally reserved for states in certain situations. 
• Such flexibility ensures effective governance and compliance with **international obligations**. 
• **Important Examples:** 
• The **Protection of Human Rights Act**, enacted to comply with **international human rights treaties**. 
• Legislation related to climate change like the **Energy Conservation Act** aligns with global agreements like the **Paris Agreement**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Legislative Competence:** 
• Under Article 253, Parliament holds the authority to legislate on **any subject**, including those under the State List, to give effect to international agreements. 
• This does not require prior approval from state legislatures, showcasing India’s **unitary tilt** in certain aspects of federalism. 
• **Key Examples:** 
• The **Atomic Energy Act** (1962) was enacted to fulfill obligations under international treaties concerning the peaceful use of atomic energy. 
• The **Foreign Trade Act** (1992) was implemented in response to global trade agreements. 
• **Judicial Interpretation:** 
• Indian courts have upheld the legislative power of Parliament under Article 253 in cases like **Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India** (1969). 
• This reinforces the principle that Parliament can legislate on state subjects to fulfill international obligations.
